entry.title: Select a phrase on touch with a hold and drag (#600)
entry.content:
Select a phrase on touch with a hold and drag (#600)

* Select a phrase on touch with a hold and drag

The reader started a phrase lookup from `onMouseUp` only. A touch drag sends no
`mouseup` event, so phrase selection did nothing on a phone.

`usePhraseTouchSelection` now owns the gesture. Hold one word for 350 ms to arm
the drag. Drag across the phrase. Release to look the phrase up.

The hook paints the run under the finger before it commits. Movement of more
than 10 px before the hold completes cancels the gesture, so a scroll still
scrolls. Once the hook arms the drag, it also blocks the browser callout and the
synthesized click.

`lookUpPhrase` is now the commit path for both gestures. The touch path reads
the phrase text from a Range between the two end words. The phrase text
therefore matches the text that the reader drew, in any script.

Tests: `e2e/reader-phrase-touch.spec.ts` covers a drag, a backward drag, a
scroll, and a hold on one word. `wordSpansBetween` has unit tests.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Harden the touch phrase gesture against a leaked click

Review found four holes in the first pass.

A click from the gesture can undo the whole selection. `preventDefault` on
`touchend` was the only guard, and Safari may still send the click. A capture
listener on the container now swallows one click after a commit, so WordCell
never clears the phrase that the drag just made.

A hold on one word waited for the click that a tap makes. iOS often sends none
after a long press, so the drawer never opened. The hook now clicks the word
itself, and it cancels the click of the browser.

The non-passive `touchmove` listener stayed bound for the life of the reader,
which held every scroll on the main thread. The hook now binds it at
`touchstart`, and only for a touch that starts on a word. It does not wait for
the hold: an engine marks `touchmove` non-cancelable once a scroll starts, and
`preventDefault` is then a no-op. The slop is 8 px for the same reason, which is
under the slop of both engines.

The commit stripped the drag paint before React drew the phrase highlight, so
one frame drew neither. The strip now waits for a timeout of 0 ms.

Tests: three more cases in `e2e/reader-phrase-touch.spec.ts`. A run that wraps
onto the next line. A phrase that survives the click of a tap. A drag inside one
transcript cue.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(bn): add the Bengali language pack (#581)
entry.content:
feat(bn): add the Bengali language pack (#581)

Bengali is the first Brahmic-script pack. The script needs no engine work. The
tokenizer keeps a word whole across its matras, its virama and its nuqta. It
treats the Bengali digits as boundaries.

Issue #252 says that an Indic pack must add script ranges in four places. That
statement is out of date. Issue #289 replaced every character range with a
Unicode property test. The one real gap is the danda. The manifest declares the
danda as a sentence terminator.

The pack builds against a 65% coverage gate. Every other pack clears 85%.
English Wiktionary holds 9,929 glossed Bengali headwords. Arabic has 35,941.

Against the top 5,000 wordfreq tokens, the exact key answers 38.7%. The
inflection tables raise the result to 55.8%. The morphology slice raises it to
69.7%. The limit is the vocabulary and not the morphology. A longer list of
suffixes reaches 71.4%. That list also invents false stems for the two extra
points.

A dictionary miss is not a dead end. The lookup route returns a null entry. The
caller then falls back to AI translate. A lower gate costs more LLM calls. It
does not cause failed lookups. The new coverageThreshold lever makes that trade
explicit in the build profile.

Coverage is 88.3% over the top 1,000 words. It is 81.8% over the top 2,000. The
formal vocabulary in the long tail is the part that fails.

Google publishes no bn-BD voice. The pack uses bn-IN. The flag is the globe,
because Bengali crosses a national border.

The build makes 9,929 entries, 15,650 senses and 38,857 inflections in 8.96 MB.
The cloze bank holds 3,213 rows over 1,063 target words.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(af): fold and peel the apostrophe the joiner now keeps (#430) (#577)
entry.content:
fix(af): fold and peel the apostrophe the joiner now keeps (#430) (#577)

* fix(af): fold and peel the apostrophe the joiner now keeps (#430)

Commit 2ec29ec added `extraJoiners` to the Afrikaans pack. The joiner is
correct. Three problems remain, and two of them break the build on master.

The reader props type uses `ActiveReaderWord` and never imports it. The
typecheck fails with two errors. Move the type into `types.ts`. Re-export it
from the component, because two other files import it from there.

The pack joins the apostrophe but does not fold the variants. `foto's` and
`foto’s` make two vocab keys. The type doc says to set both flags together.
Add `foldApostrophes`.

The pack declares no morphology. The joined token reaches no dictionary key,
because the dictionary holds `foto` and not `foto's`. Add an `'s` clitic peel.
`vocabKeys` keeps only a candidate that peels an apostrophe. A plural with no
apostrophe cannot fire this peel.

Update the two tests that the joiner changed. Move the Afrikaans apostrophe
sentences out of the legacy parity corpus, as Italian did for its elisions.
Add pack goldens for the plural, the fold, the peel, and the quote mark.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(af): cover the ABC's and 1990's cases from #430

The issue names an abbreviation plural and a decade plural next to foto's.
Digits and capitals are word characters, so the joiner keeps both whole. Assert
it, and assert that each one peels to its base key.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(af): correct the note about the Dutch split

The first version repeated a claim from the fr and nl manifests. That claim
says the avoidWords clitic fragments depend on the apostrophe split. The
dependency runs the other way. The split makes the fragments.

Italian is the evidence. It joined the apostrophe in #548 and kept l, d, all,
dell, nell and sull in its avoidWords list, because wordfreq and older vocab
rows still carry them. So a joiner can land in the Dutch pack with no rework.

entry.title: feat(reader): configurable prose style, global and per language (#570…
entry.content:
feat(reader): configurable prose style, global and per language (#570) (#571)

* feat(reader): configurable prose style, global and per language (#570)

The reader drew every language at one size, one weight, one kerning and one
leading. A script does not read well at one setting. Japanese sits inside the em
box and writes no spaces, so a leading tuned for Latin leaves its lines too far
apart.

Three layers now decide how a lesson is drawn, and each field resolves on its
own:

1. The language pack (`script.prose`) says what the script needs.
2. The reader's global setting applies in every language.
3. The reader's per-language setting applies in one language.

A later layer wins. A pack default never overrules a stated preference, and a
global preference never overrules a per-language one.

The resolved values reach the DOM as custom properties on the reader container.
The article, the transcript reader and every word chip read them by
inheritance, so no component takes a new prop.

Settings gets a "Reading text" panel with a scope selector, four sliders and a
live sample in the pack's own script. A per-language edit stores only the field
that moved, so everything else keeps following the global setting.

Japanese now ships a pack leading of 1.6. That is the language the issue
reports.

Other notes:

- An overhanging annotation (furigana) takes its room from the gap between the
  lines, and the browser reserves none. The annotated leading is the resolved
  leading plus a per-script extra. A floor of 1.75 holds it there, so a tight
  setting cannot drop the furigana onto the line above. An in-flow annotation is
  already part of the line box, and pinyin therefore takes no floor.
- The defaults draw a Latin lesson exactly as before: 20px, weight 700, kerning
  0, leading 1.9. The reader used to step from 18px to 20px at the `sm`
  breakpoint. One value now covers both widths, because a size the reader chose
  must not change under it at a breakpoint.
- The settings live in browser storage, browser-scoped, the same choice the
  theme makes. The right font size is a property of the screen, not of the
  account.
- A word chip with no click handler no longer takes button semantics. The panel
  preview draws chips with nothing to look up.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(reader): measure the furigana floor, and save the sliders explicitly (#570)

Three corrections after reading the panel and the Japanese reader on screen.

The furigana floor was wrong. It was 1.75, derived from the 1.0em Han square
plus the 0.58em reading. What has to fit is the word CHIP. A chip is an inline
box, so its height is the reading font's content area, about 1.4em for
Literata. Measured in Chrome at 20px, 26px and 32px, the reading first clears
the line above at 2.15, and by 0.4px. The floor is now 2.3, which is the first
value with daylight in it.

2.15 is also what the reader hardcoded before #570, so that layout was always
one rounding error from a collision.

Japanese moves from 1.6 to 1.7. 1.6 read as cramped with the annotations off.

The sliders now write a draft, and Save applies it. The sample in the panel
follows every drag, so the effect is visible before the reader changes. Reset
throws away the unsaved sliders and whatever the scope holds in storage. A draft is
held per scope, so a reader who edits Japanese, looks at German and comes back
still has their edit.

The per-field marker was the accent colour, which read as a button. It is muted
now, and it says which language it belongs to.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(settings): address the Anthropic credential controls by test id

The reading typography panel (#570) put a second Save button on the settings
page, above the credential one. settings-credentials.spec.ts reached its own
button with getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).first(). It found the new one
instead, waited for a disabled control, and timed out.

The Anthropic credential block never got the test ids its OpenAI twin has. Add
them with the same names, then address them from the spec. The names are
anthropic-api-key, -save, -status, -replace, -clear and -cancel.

A settings page can hold more than one Save button. A label lookup was therefore
always fragile here. A test id is not.

entry.title: feat(billing): apply a Paddle discount to in-app checkout (#516) (#568)
entry.content:
feat(billing): apply a Paddle discount to in-app checkout (#516) (#568)

Lector Cloud had no way to apply a discount, which blocked every promotion
and win-back offer. Paddle now holds each discount. The app holds only a
map from a code word to a Paddle discount id.

- Add PADDLE_DISCOUNT_CODES, a JSON map of code word to `dsc_…` id. Unset
  means coupons stay off.
- A bad entry warns and drops. It never stops the boot. A broken map gives
  nobody a discount, which is the safe direction.
- POST /api/billing/checkout takes an optional `promo`. It answers with
  `discount: applied`, `unknown`, or `none`.
- makePaddleTransactionCreator sends `discount_id`. Paddle prices the
  transaction, so the overlay opens on the discounted total.
- The browser can never send a discount id. A Paddle code word holds
  letters and numbers only, so a `dsc_…` value cannot become a lookup key.
  A test asserts this.
- An unknown code stops the redirect. The reader stays on the plan picker
  and reads why. A redirect shows them a price they did not expect, which
  is the one outcome to avoid.
- sanitizeAuthReturnPath now allows `plan` and `promo`. It rebuilds the
  destination from validated values. An unknown or repeated parameter
  rejects the whole destination.

entry.title: Vocab/bulk delete (#569)
entry.content:
Vocab/bulk delete (#569)

* fix(email): the API field is fallback_value, not fallbackValue

Every template variable has carried a null fallback since #558. The REST API
names the field `fallback_value`. This script sent `fallbackValue`, which Resend
accepts, ignores, and answers 200 to. The Node SDK converts the case. This
script calls fetch directly, so it does not.

A null fallback is not cosmetic. It is the only guard on a send that omits a
variable, and without one Resend renders the variable as nothing. That means an
empty headline, an empty word count, or an empty `src` on the language
screenshot, which every client shows as a broken image.

A fallback also only reaches the live template through a publish. A PATCH alone
updates the draft, and a GET keeps returning the published values, which is why
this looked unfixable at first.

Add verifyPublished, which reads each template back after its publish and warns
if a variable the body uses is undeclared or has no fallback, or if the subject
does not match. It sets a non-zero exit code. Nothing in the old output could
have revealed a silently dropped field.

Verified against the live templates: all six now report every variable with a
fallback, and day-1 reads back all seven.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* add new bulk-delete endpoint

* add data-layer consumer for bulk delete endpoint

* add bulk-delete functionality to vocab page

* add max length to req and wrap it in a transaction

* add malformed json req guard

* update PR feedback

* update

* hoist db ops

* test(vocab): cover bulk delete, and document it in the OpenAPI spec

The endpoint had no tests. Most of these cover the knownWords half rather
than the vocab half, because that is where bulk delete and DELETE /:id can
drift apart: the single-row route drops the knownWords entry when no other
vocab row in that language folds to the same key, and a batch has to reach
the same end state.

Cases that earn their place:

  - an unknown id must not abandon the ids after it. The loop body is a
    callback today, so `return` skips one item. Under a for-of it would
    abandon the batch, which no other assertion detects.
  - HAEUSER and haeuser are one folded key (#289), so deleting either alone
    must leave the knownWords row standing.
  - a mixed-language batch sweeps each language on its own, and a language
    absent from the batch stays untouched.
  - a bare string carries .length, so only the Array.isArray clause stops it
    reaching the id loop and answering 500.

user-scoping.test.ts asks every route to prove it cannot see another
tenant. Two cases there: another user's id is skipped rather than deleted,
and their identical word neither saves nor loses a knownWords row, which
pins the userId scope on the survivor scan.

The e2e spec covers the button, the confirm, and select-all across pages.

The OpenAPI ratchet fails any route missing from annotations.ts, and this
route was missing, so add its entry and regenerate openapi.json.

entry.title: feat(email): rewrite the lifecycle copy for retention (#565)
entry.content:
feat(email): rewrite the lifecycle copy for retention (#565)

The day 1 mail told the reader something false about their own account, and
two mails told German and Spanish learners their library was empty when it
holds twenty-two seeded lessons. Both cost trust at exactly the moment these
mails exist to keep it.

Day 1 fires on savedWordCount === 0 and checks nothing else, but the copy said
"you haven't created any lessons yet". That is false for anybody who imported a
book and read it without saving a word, and the send cannot know it either way.
The mail now names what the trigger measures, which is the saved word.

Starter content is the second correction. #315 seeds a graded series into the
library on first language selection, and de and es are the two packs that ship
one. So a Resend template cannot state the library's state, because the true
sentence differs per language. Add a STARTER_LINE variable that
lifecycle-email.ts composes from hasStarterContent(), and print it instead.

Add WORD_COUNT for the same reason. The Anki mail fires at ten saved words and
described that as "a modest word list", which is vague where it could be exact
and faintly disparaging about the reader's own effort.

Copy changes across all five:

- Stronger subject lines. "Just checking in" and "Need a hand with your first
  lesson?" earned no open. No variable goes in a subject the app sends
  automatically, because an interpolation failure would reach real users
  silently.
- Less apology. "No rush" twice, "when you have a moment", "if that helps" and
  "a modest word list" are gone. Each one gave the reader permission to ignore
  the mail.
- More help. Every mail now asks the reader to reply if they have an issue, and
  says the reply is read.
- Day 3 loses the video. A reader can receive welcome, day 1 and day 3, and all
  three carried the same thumbnail. It also no longer tells them to pick a
  language, which hasRealUse implies they may have done already.
- The gloss cap mail leads with what still works, then names one action. It
  previously offered three exits in one sentence, with self-hosting before the
  bring-your-own-key route.
- Every mail addresses the reader by name. Only the welcome did.

Also restores the language-request-notification template, which lived only in
Resend and in an untracked local file, so nothing in the repository described
what is published. It carries a per-language screenshot through a
SCREENSHOT_URL variable.

Adds `--print`, which renders the copy with no network call and no API key.
`--dry-run` lists the live templates first, so it cannot show the wording
before a key exists, and reading the wording is the common case.

Verified: 28 lifecycle-email tests pass, including three new ones for
starterLine. The 15 failures in api/src/lib are the pre-existing missing
@sglkc/kuromoji dependency. tsc --noEmit is clean.

entry.title: feat(ar): Arabic language pack (#253) (#562)
entry.content:
feat(ar): Arabic language pack (#253) (#562)

* feat(ar): Arabic language pack (#253)

Arabic is the first right-to-left pack. It is also the first pack with a
script that hides part of the word. Unvocalized text omits every short
vowel.

The dump is not the shape the issue expects. #253 expects vocalized
headwords. Only 30 of 77,339 carry a diacritic. The vocalized spelling
sits on the `canonical` form row instead, on 99.2% of glossed entries.

So the key needs no help to match running text. The vocalized form
becomes data worth a column. It goes in `ipa`, which is where a lookup
prints it.

`sounds[]` cannot do that job. It covers 20,695 entries. Every tag on it
names a dialect: Hijazi, Moroccan, Egyptian, Kuwaiti. A selection from it
ships a regional reading into a pack for Modern Standard Arabic.

Results: 25,750 entries, 58,893 senses, 347,672 inflections, 49.6 MB.
Coverage is 98.7% of the top 4,822 wordfreq-ar tokens. The cloze bank
holds 7,126 rows over 1,680 target words.

New levers in the build profile:

- `foldArabicKeys` drops the tashkeel and the tatweel. It also folds the
  four alef spellings onto bare alef. `stripFromKeys` cannot do this.
  That lever strips on the NFD form. NFD takes ؤ and ئ apart as well as
  أ. So a strip wide enough for the alef also folds the waw and the ya.
- `readingFromCanonicalForm` reads the vocalized spelling off the
  canonical row.
- `looseAliases` registers the ة/ه and ى/ي variant of every key as an
  alias row. Step 3-ar in the lookup retries against those rows.
- `leadFormsRel` names which lemma leads a folded key.

The lead map answers a real defect. Unvocalized Arabic spells several
words the same way, so 6,133 of 25,747 keys hold more than one lemma.
Only 341 of those come from the alef fold. The other 5,792 are the
script itself, and no keying choice avoids them.

Every lemma's senses merge under the one key, so the pack loses nothing.
But the order is the dump's etymology order. For a short list of very
frequent words that order leads with a rare verb. `ان` is the fourth most
frequent word in the language, and it led with آن "time" in place of the
conjunction أَنْ. `لم` led with لَمَّ "to gather" in place of the
negator.

The map holds 14 keys, curated against the top 200 of the corpus. If a
key matches no record, the build fails, so the map cannot rot against a
later dump. 15 reading invariants guard the result.

The morphology slice peels both ends of the word. Arabic writes its
conjunctions, prepositions and article onto the front with no space, and
they stack: وبالقلم is و + ب + ال + قلم. `maxPrefixes` is new for that,
because one pass stops at بالقلم, which is not a key.

`minStem` is 2 and not 3. Arabic writes a proclitic onto its shortest
words most often. A floor of 3 refused وهو, ومن, ففي and بكل. Those were
17 of the 89 coverage misses.

This also fixes a trap in the lookup. The mark-stripped fallback read
`practiceLeniency` as its trigger. The two are unrelated. Leniency says
what a typed practice answer may omit. That step needs the alias rows
only the grc build profile writes.

Arabic must set leniency, because a learner types no tashkeel, so Arabic
inherited the stripping. NFD takes the hamza carriers apart. 817 Arabic
entries change under it, and 51 of them reach a DIFFERENT entry. A lookup
of رؤية "seeing" answered روية "deliberation". The step now selects on
